newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS - Czech cbank rate cut fails to weaken crown.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Czech cbank rate cut fails to weaken crown.

text.p: The Czech National Bank on Thursday slashed its Lombard lending rate in its biggest step to date in easing its grip on the embattled crown, but the currency withstood predictions it would weaken on the cut.
The CNB said that effective June 27, the Lombard rate, its last resort lending facility for banks, would fall to 23 percent from a previous 50 percent.

"After the currency volatility, which forced currency and interest rate intervention and led the the freeing up of the currency, the situation on the finanical markets is gradually stabilising," a CNB statement said.
"This allows for the gradual reduction of interest rates on the interbank market," it added.
The statement made no mention of the discount rate, which was raised to 13 percent from 10.5 percent during the crown crisis.

On May 16, the CNB hiked the Lombard rate to 50 percent from 14 percent in an attempt to shore up the sagging crown after several waves of direct intervention failed to stem downward pressure brought about by a wave of short-selling.
Dealers had predicted in recent weeks that the crown could weaken sharply and possibly face another attack if rates were lowered, but the currency held its ground immediately after the cut.
At 1340 GMT the crown was trading at 18.486 to the mark from 18.489 at the time of the announcement.
Traders said that despite the cut, Czech interest rates remained high and that there would be little heavy pressure on the currency in the near term.

"After the news I would have expected it (the crown) to have weakened by about 50 basis points...Still the rates are basically high and we don't think it (the crown) can go down much in the near term," said Petr Kukla of Girocredit Bank.
The central bank was eventually forced to float the crown because of the crisis, and has since kept rates high to choke market liquidity and halt any major slide of the currency.
Over the past two weeks, the CNB has been gradually lossening its grip on the crown as the speculative pressure eased.

The central bank has lifted an informal agreement it had with banks to limit non-resident access to the local money market last month, and lowered its repo rate to 18.5 percent on Thursday after it peaked during the crisis at 75 percent.
